name: Mewing

lead: Mewing is a do-it-yourself habit of keeping the tongue flat against the roof of the mouth, lips closed and teeth lightly together, with nasal breathing. It is named after the British orthodontist John Mew and his son Mike Mew, who promoted a wider approach called orthotropics. It spread widely on social media from 2019 and became one of the best-known practices in looksmaxxing communities.

Proponents say sustained tongue posture can push the upper jaw forward and sharpen the jawline, with the strongest effects claimed in children. Orthodontic bodies say no credible research shows it reshapes the face. The one controlled study usually cited is a small twin study of orthotropic versus conventional braces treatment, which tested professional orthotropic appliances rather than tongue posture alone.

paras: The theory holds that the tongue's resting pressure on the palate guides upper-jaw growth forward and outward, and that jaw shape depends heavily on posture and breathing habits rather than genetics alone. Mainstream orthodontics attributes facial form mainly to genetics and growth. Some community members also say the posture temporarily lifts the hyoid bone and tightens the area under the chin, which can change how the jawline looks.

Gentle tongue posture is not documented to carry serious risks, though some online posts report masseter enlargement or a worse appearance from forceful versions. The main documented harms concern Mike Mew's clinical practice, which a UK regulatory tribunal examined, rather than the home technique. Orthodontic organizations warn that it may delay evidence-based treatment for real bite or jaw problems.

lead: Mewing is a self-directed practice in which a person rests the whole tongue against the roof of the mouth, keeps the lips sealed and the teeth lightly together, and breathes through the nose, with the stated aim of improving jaw and facial structure [1][1]. It takes its name from John Mew, a British orthodontist, and his son Mike Mew, who promoted the approach known as orthotropics [2][3].

Orthotropics holds that oral posture, especially tongue position, guides facial growth, and that crooked teeth and recessed jaws are largely environmental. Professional orthodontic bodies do not support this, and Wikipedia describes mewing as an unproven or pseudoscientific technique [2][3]. The American Association of Orthodontists has stated there is no evidence that mewing improves the jaw [3].

Interest in mewing rose sharply from January 2019, spreading through social media and looksmaxxing forums [3]. A 2019 commentary in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery concluded that it is not a viable alternative to orthognathic surgery [4][2]. Proponents continue to report benefits, particularly for people who began in childhood.

paras: The technique is usually described as pressing the full length of the tongue, including the back third, flat against the palate, with the lips closed, the teeth lightly touching or close together without clenching, and attention to nasal breathing and neck posture [1][1]. Proponents describe it as a resting posture to be held throughout the day rather than a timed exercise.

Online communities distinguish ordinary mewing from 'hard mewing', in which people press the tongue upward with more force, and from combinations with other practices such as chewing, chin tucks and mouth taping.

John Mew, born in 1928, qualified in dentistry at University College London in 1953. In 1958 he put forward the 'Tropic Premise', which treats malocclusion as a postural problem that early intervention can prevent [2]. He developed orthotropics, including the Biobloc appliance combining a palate expander with a postural appliance, and in 1987 helped found the International Association of Facial Growth Guidance in Fort Worth, Texas [2]. Grokipedia traces related ideas to early twentieth-century myofunctional therapy and the London School of Facial Orthotropics, founded in 1983 [1].

Mew's views drew opposition from mainstream British orthodontists. In the late 1980s the NHS fined him for inappropriate treatment, but he won a High Court appeal in 1987. The General Dental Council reprimanded him in 2010 over misleading advertising and revoked his licence in 2017 [2]. He died on 25 June 2025 [2].

Mike Mew promoted tongue posture to a wide audience online, and the term 'mewing' emerged in online communities during the 2010s [1]. Google search interest began rising in January 2019, followed by media coverage including The Guardian and, in 2020, a New York Times Magazine profile of the Mews and their following [3]. The practice spread particularly within looksmaxxing and incel subcultures [3].
The British Orthodontic Society expelled Mike Mew around 2018 to 2019, and in 2024 he was struck from the UK dental register after a tribunal examined his treatment of child patients [3][2][1].
No controlled trial has tested tongue posture alone, as practised in mewing, for changing facial structure.

A small controlled study of 12 identical twins compared fixed orthodontic appliances with orthotropic (growth guidance) treatment without fixed appliances, assessed ten years later by 12 lay judges. Most conventionally treated twins were judged less attractive after treatment, while most orthotropically treated twins were judged improved, and the traditionally treated cases relapsed more often [5]. The study examined professionally delivered orthotropic treatment, not self-directed mewing.

A 2019 commentary in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery examined mewing as an alternative to orthognathic surgery [4], and a 2026 article in the Journal of Clinical Orthodontics discussed the mewing trend [6]. A 1992 paper by an orthodontic author put forward hypotheses that tongue and lip posture influence oropharyngeal development and Eustachian tube function, proposing that early orthotropic treatment might direct growth forward; it reports clinical impressions rather than a controlled trial [7].

The American Association of Orthodontists published an explainer in March 2025 stating there is no evidence that mewing reshapes the jaw [3]. Wikipedia reports that most orthodontists do not regard it as a viable alternative to jaw surgery [2][3]. Grokipedia, which is AI-generated, states that authoritative sources see facial structure as determined mainly by genetics and growth and mentions possible risks including temporomandibular joint problems, tooth misalignment and bite issues, but these are not backed by a cited study there [1]. Proponents counter that orthotropics rests on a different view of growth in which posture and breathing shape the face, and that mainstream orthodontics is too focused on teeth [1].

Mewing is among the most discussed practices on looksmax.org, with threads from users reporting results, others describing none, and others suggesting it matters mainly in early adolescence [8][9]. One user's thread title describes mewing as having 'ruined' their face, while another claims it works and offers a how-to [10][11]. A 2025 qualitative study of an online looksmaxxing community analysed 8,072 comments and noted that the community encourages substantial body modification such as mewing and leg lengthening, and argued that participation harms users' health [12].
The word is also used as slang. Some people say 'mewing' in jest, or describe a 'mewing face', and students reportedly mew in class to avoid answering questions [3].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, mewing is treated as a baseline practice that members debate constantly, with advice about age cut-offs, hard mewing, and how it combines with chewing or palate expansion [8][13].
